title: Ergonomics and manual handling
moduleTitle: Shared: Job management and service delivery
audience: Trainee or new worker on the window cleaning (all heights) track, working under supervision.
learningOutcomes: Plan loads, routes and movement before lifting or carrying.
Use carts and adjustable tools to keep loads close and avoid twisting under load.
Report tasks that exceed personal capacity and choose a safer system of work.

instruction.heading: Exterior, height and access context
instruction.body: This lesson is part of the window cleaning (all heights) track. The track covers ground-level, water-fed pole and elevated access work on glazing and frames. Any work above ground level, or from a ladder, scaffold or elevating work platform, is restricted: it needs employer authorisation under a site-specific risk assessment, and the worker must hold any licence the relevant state or territory requires for the equipment used. This lesson does not grant the right to work at height or on solar systems.

instruction.heading: Instruction
instruction.body: Set handles and trolley loads to reduce strain; plan lifting, carrying and repetitive tasks.

instruction.heading: Learning goal and job context
instruction.body: This lesson teaches ergonomics and manual handling for routine cleaning work. Start with the actual job scope, site instructions, manufacturer directions and worker training. Never treat a general lesson as authority to perform restricted or specialist work.

instruction.heading: Core procedure
instruction.body: Plan loads and movement before lifting. Use carts and adjustable tools, keep loads close, avoid twisting under load and break up repetitive work. Manual-handling controls depend on the task and worker; do not teach a single lifting posture as a guarantee against injury.

instruction.heading: Decision-making in the field
instruction.body: Before acting, ask: What is the surface or equipment? What is the soil or hazard? Which product or method is approved? What could harm a person, property or food? If the answer is unclear, pause, protect the area and seek supervisor guidance.

instruction.heading: Worked workplace scenario
instruction.body: A cleaner carries two full buckets up stairs. They assess load, route and safer transport arrangements before proceeding.

instruction.heading: Guided supervised practice
instruction.body: Complete a task-risk review and demonstrate cart setup, handle adjustment and controlled movement.

instruction.heading: Evidence and feedback
instruction.body: The assessor observes the task and checks whether the learner: chooses safer systems and reports tasks beyond personal capacity. A learner must explain any unsafe choice, correct it and repeat the demonstration. Record observations, required coaching and reassessment rather than awarding competence from attendance alone.

instruction.heading: Stop-work rule
instruction.body: Stop-work rule: stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

procedure: Plan the load, the route and the movement before lifting or carrying.
Use carts and adjustable tools, and set handles and trolley loads to reduce strain.
Keep loads close to the body, and avoid twisting while carrying a load.
Assess a heavy or awkward load, such as two full buckets on stairs, and choose a safer transport arrangement before going up.
Break up repetitive work where practicable.
Report any task that is beyond your personal capacity, and agree a safer system of work with the supervisor.
Do not rely on one lifting posture as a guarantee against injury; choose the method for the task and the worker.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Licence and height notice: This lesson does not grant the right to work at height, on roofs, from elevated work platforms, or on solar systems. Completing it is not a licence, certificate or authority for regulated work. Boom-type elevating work platforms need a high risk work licence in Victoria at any boom length, and in New South Wales, Queensland, Tasmania, the Northern Territory and Western Australia where the boom is 11 metres or more. The WorkSafe WA page (last updated 13 August 2026) and the NT WorkSafe bulletin (no date shown) both state the 11-metre threshold. Check whether this work needs a high-risk work licence with the state regulator before you start. Queensland's definition does not cover platforms under 11 metres (WorkSafe Queensland page, no date shown). Tasmania's WP licence applies where the boom length is 11 metres or more, and no licence is needed for a boom under 11 metres (WorkSafe Tasmania page, last updated 1 December 2023). In New South Wales and Queensland the boom length is 11 metres: a boom-type platform of 11 metres or more needs the licence, and a shorter boom may not need it in those states. Victoria's WP class has no boom-length threshold, so the licence is not limited by length there. This lesson does not grant a licence. Scissor lifts need no high risk work licence in Victoria or the Northern Territory. Check the licence rules for your state or territory and obtain your employer's written authorisation before any work above ground level.

Stop-work rule: stop immediately, make the area safe, and tell your supervisor before resuming if the surface, anchor, ladder, platform or roof is unstable or uncertain; wind, rain, ice or fading light changes conditions; you see or suspect exposed wiring, damaged cable, water near electrical equipment or live parts; a person or animal enters the exclusion zone; the task falls outside your training, authorisation or the work order; or you are asked to work above ground level without the licence or authorisation required.

qualityStandard: Loads, routes and movement are planned before lifting or carrying.
Carts and adjustable tools are used, loads are kept close, and twisting under load is avoided.
Repetitive work is broken up where practicable.
Tasks beyond personal capacity are reported, and a safer system of work is chosen.
summary: Loads, routes and movement are planned before any lifting or carrying, and handles and trolley loads are set to reduce strain.
Carts and adjustable tools keep loads close, and twisting under load is avoided.
A task that exceeds personal capacity is reported and a safer system of work is chosen, because no single lifting posture guarantees protection from injury.

knowledgeChecks.question: What should you check before performing ergonomics and manual handling?
options: Whether you can carry more buckets in one trip and whether the buckets fit the van
That one lifting posture is a guarantee against injury and that the crew can work fast
Whether the buckets are full to the top and whether the stairs are wet
The load, the route, and whether a cart or assistance is needed before lifting

knowledgeChecks.question: What do you do when a load is too awkward to lift alone?
options: Twist to place the load in the van and lift it up from the ground at once
Lift it quickly to get it over with and do not stop to rest until it is done
Lift it alone, then report the strain later and carry on with the rest of the room
Use a safer system such as a cart or assistance, and report tasks beyond your capacity

knowledgeChecks.question: What should you do before carrying two full buckets up a flight of stairs?
options: Carry both buckets up the stairs at once to save a trip today
Ask nobody and let the load settle on the stairs while the crew watches
Hold one bucket on each hip and climb quickly and do not stop on the way up
Assess the load, the route and a safer transport arrangement before going up

knowledgeChecks.question: Which manual-handling practice is unsafe?
options: Using a cart on suitable ground for the team
Keeping loads close to the body when lifting
Breaking up repetitive work with short breaks
Carrying two full buckets up the stairs at once

knowledgeChecks.question: What should you report when a task is beyond personal capacity?
options: Report the task that is beyond personal capacity so a safer system can be arranged
Note nothing, since manual handling is personal and nobody needs a record of it
Ask a client to lift for you and the client is happy to help you lift it
Keep the excess load to yourself and carry on with the job alone until it is done
